title: Traditional Gender Roles
rootClaim: Traditional gender roles are social constructs that restrict individual freedom, perpetuate gender inequality, and should be dismantled in modern society.

branches.text: Social Constructivism: Gender roles are culturally enforced behavioral expectations that artificially constrain individual potential regardless of biological sex.

children.text: Performativity Theory: Judith Butler argues gender is not an internal essence but a continuous series of socially coerced cultural performances.

Cross-Cultural Evolutionary Universals: Specific labor divisions (e.g., male physical defense/hunting, female child-nurturing) evolved independently across isolated human societies, pointing to biological underpinnings.
Technological Decoupling: Industrialization, artificial infant formula, and modern reproductive control render ancestral physical division of labor obsolete.
Hormonal & Neurological Dimorphism: Prenatal androgen exposure systematically influences personality traits like risk tolerance, spatial processing, and occupational interest patterns.
Psychological Harm to Men: Rigid traditional masculinity ('toxic masculinity') discourages emotional vulnerability, leading to elevated male suicide rates and resistance to mental healthcare.

branches.text: Evolutionary Psychology & Functionalism: Traditional gender roles reflect complementary biological adaptations that optimize family stability and reproductive success.

children.text: Gender Equality Paradox: In Scandinavian countries with high gender equity, sex differences in STEM vs caretaking career choices increase rather than decrease.
Confounding Structural Pressures: Even egalitarian welfare states retain subtle cultural biases and tax structures that nudge women toward flexible public sector jobs.

definitions.description: Judith Butler's theory that gender is produced through repeated stylized acts rather than being an innate biological identity.
The empirical finding that personality and occupational choice differences between men and women are larger in more gender-equal societies.
The perspective that human development and concepts of reality are socially situated and built through cooperative cultural norms.
Systematic differences in physical form or psychological traits between individuals of different biological sexes in the same species.
